questions.prompt: Assigning one struct variable to another copies all of its fields, so changing a field on the copy does not affect the original.
questions.explanation: True. Structs are value types, so assignment copies the whole value. The two variables then hold independent data, unlike class references that point to the same object.

questions.prompt: `string` is a value type in C#, which is why two strings with the same characters compare equal with `==`.
questions.explanation: False. `string` (System.String) is a reference type. It compares by content with `==` only because the type overloads the equality operators to compare characters.

questions.prompt: Calling `s.Replace("a", "b")` changes the characters stored in the string `s`.
questions.explanation: False. Strings are immutable, so `Replace` returns a new string and leaves the original untouched. You must assign the result, e.g. `s = s.Replace("a", "b")`.

questions.prompt: Assigning an `int` to a variable of type `object` allocates a new object on the heap that holds a copy of the value.
questions.explanation: True. This is boxing: the runtime allocates a heap object and copies the value into it. Unboxing copies it back out, and both add allocation and GC cost in hot paths.

questions.prompt: Two instances of the same `record class` type whose properties all hold equal values compare equal with `==`.
questions.explanation: True. Records have compiler-generated value equality: `Equals`, `==` and `GetHashCode` compare the members instead of the references. Ordinary classes compare by reference unless you override equality.

questions.prompt: A positional `record struct` such as `record struct Point(int X, int Y);` is immutable, just like a positional `record class`.
questions.explanation: False. For a positional `record struct` the compiler generates read-write properties (`get; set;`). Only a `readonly record struct` gets init-only properties like a positional `record class` does.

questions.prompt: A `with` expression on a record creates a copy with the specified properties changed and leaves the original instance unchanged.
questions.explanation: True. `p with { X = 5 }` clones the record and then applies the listed changes to the clone. This is nondestructive mutation; the source instance is not modified.

questions.prompt: With nullable reference types enabled, the runtime throws an exception when `null` is assigned to a variable declared as non-nullable `string`.
questions.explanation: False. Nullable reference types are a compile-time feature: the compiler issues warnings, but nothing is checked at run time. A `string` variable can still hold `null` if warnings are ignored or suppressed.

questions.prompt: The null-forgiving operator `!` only suppresses compiler nullability warnings and adds no null check at run time.
questions.explanation: True. `x!` tells the compiler to treat `x` as not null; it has no runtime effect. If `x` is actually null, you will still get a `NullReferenceException` later when it is dereferenced.

questions.prompt: Calling `Where` on an `IEnumerable<T>` does not run the filter until the result is enumerated.
questions.explanation: True. `Where` uses deferred execution: it returns a query object, and the predicate runs only when something like `foreach`, `ToList()` or `Count()` enumerates it.

questions.prompt: Enumerating the same deferred LINQ query twice runs it only once, because the first enumeration caches the results.
questions.explanation: False. A deferred query is re-executed on every enumeration, so its source is read and its predicates run again each time. Call `ToList()` or `ToArray()` to materialize the results once.

questions.prompt: A `Where` applied to an EF Core `IQueryable<T>` is translated into SQL, but the same `Where` applied after `AsEnumerable()` filters the rows in memory.
questions.explanation: True. `IQueryable<T>` builds an expression tree that the provider translates into the database query. After `AsEnumerable()` the rest of the query uses LINQ to Objects, so every row is fetched first and then filtered on the client.

questions.prompt: A `List<int>` stores its elements without boxing them.
questions.explanation: True. Generic collections are specialized for value types, so `List<int>` keeps the values in an internal `int[]`. The non-generic `ArrayList` is the one that boxes every `int`.

questions.prompt: Like Java, C# erases generic type arguments at compile time, so at run time `List<int>` and `List<string>` are the same type.
questions.explanation: False. .NET generics are reified: the runtime knows the type arguments, so `typeof(List<int>) != typeof(List<string>)`, and `typeof(T)` works inside generic code. Value-type instantiations even get their own specialized native code.

questions.prompt: A `switch` expression that does not handle every possible input compiles with a warning and throws a `SwitchExpressionException` at run time if no arm matches.
questions.explanation: True. The compiler reports a non-exhaustive switch expression as a warning, not an error. If no pattern matches at run time, the generated code throws `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.SwitchExpressionException`.

questions.prompt: If a class overloads `==`, the pattern `x is null` calls that overloaded operator.
questions.explanation: False. `is null` is a constant pattern that always does a plain reference (or `HasValue`) check and ignores user-defined operators. That is why `is null` is the reliable null test even when `==` is overloaded.
True. This is a declaration pattern: it tests the runtime type and, on success, assigns the converted value to the new variable `c`, which is definitely assigned inside the `if` block.

questions.prompt: Newly allocated small objects start in generation 0 of the managed heap.
questions.explanation: True. Small objects are allocated in generation 0, and objects that survive a collection are promoted to generation 1 and then generation 2. Most objects die young, so gen 0 collections are cheap and frequent.

questions.prompt: An object of 85,000 bytes or more is allocated in generation 0 like any other new object.
questions.explanation: False. Objects of 85,000 bytes or more go to the large object heap (LOH), which is logically part of generation 2 and collected only with gen 2 collections. That makes large short-lived allocations relatively expensive.

questions.prompt: Calling `Dispose()` on an object makes the garbage collector reclaim that object's memory immediately.
questions.explanation: False. `Dispose` releases resources such as file handles or connections deterministically, but the object's managed memory is reclaimed only later, when the GC finds it unreachable.

questions.prompt: An unreachable object with a finalizer survives at least one extra garbage collection, because its finalizer must run before its memory can be reclaimed.
questions.explanation: True. When the GC finds a finalizable object unreachable, it queues it for the finalizer thread and keeps it alive, promoting it. The memory is freed only by a later collection, which is why `Dispose` patterns call `GC.SuppressFinalize`.

questions.prompt: A Native AOT app still ships with a JIT compiler so it can compile code it discovers at run time, such as assemblies loaded with `Assembly.LoadFile`.
questions.explanation: False. Native AOT apps contain no JIT: all code is compiled ahead of time. Dynamic loading of assemblies and runtime code generation such as `System.Reflection.Emit` are not supported.

questions.prompt: Publishing with Native AOT produces a self-contained native executable that runs without a separately installed .NET runtime.
questions.explanation: True. Native AOT compiles the app and the parts of the runtime it needs into a single native binary for the target platform. The target machine does not need the .NET runtime installed.

questions.prompt: Marking a method `async` makes it run on a background thread.
questions.explanation: False. An `async` method runs synchronously on the caller's thread until its first `await` of an incomplete task. `async` only enables `await`; use `Task.Run` if you actually want work on the thread pool.

questions.prompt: ASP.NET Core has no `SynchronizationContext`, so code after an `await` in a controller may resume on a different thread-pool thread.
questions.explanation: True. Unlike classic ASP.NET, ASP.NET Core does not install a synchronization context. Continuations run on any thread-pool thread, so you cannot rely on thread affinity across awaits.

questions.prompt: Blocking on `task.Result` in an ASP.NET Core controller deadlocks because the continuation waits for the request's `SynchronizationContext`, exactly as in classic ASP.NET.
questions.explanation: False. ASP.NET Core has no `SynchronizationContext`, so that classic context deadlock does not occur. Blocking on async code is still harmful because it ties up thread-pool threads and can lead to thread-pool starvation under load.

questions.prompt: `await task.ConfigureAwait(false)` makes the awaited operation itself run on a thread-pool thread.
questions.explanation: False. `ConfigureAwait(false)` does not change where the awaited operation runs. It only tells the awaiter not to resume the continuation on the captured synchronization context or task scheduler.

questions.prompt: A `ValueTask<T>` can safely be awaited multiple times, just like a `Task<T>`.
questions.explanation: False. A `ValueTask<T>` may be backed by a pooled, reusable source, so it should be awaited only once. If you need to await it more than once, convert it with `AsTask()` first.

questions.prompt: An exception thrown inside an `async void` method cannot be caught by a `try`/`catch` around the call, because the caller gets no `Task` to observe.
questions.explanation: True. Exceptions from `async void` methods are raised directly on the synchronization context (or thread pool) and can crash the process. That is why `async void` should be limited to event handlers.

questions.prompt: When several tasks passed to `Task.WhenAll` fail, `await Task.WhenAll(...)` throws an `AggregateException` containing all of their exceptions.
questions.explanation: False. `await` unwraps the aggregate and rethrows only the first exception. All exceptions are still available through the returned task's `Exception` property, which is an `AggregateException`.

questions.prompt: A service registered as transient gets a new instance every time it is resolved from the container.
questions.explanation: True. Transient services are created each time they are requested, singletons once for the app, and scoped services once per scope (per request in ASP.NET Core).

questions.prompt: A scoped service in ASP.NET Core is shared across all requests from the same user session.
questions.explanation: False. In ASP.NET Core a scope is created per HTTP request, so a scoped service lives for one request. Sessions have nothing to do with DI lifetimes.

questions.prompt: In the Development environment, the default ASP.NET Core host throws an exception when a singleton service depends on a scoped service.
questions.explanation: True. Scope validation is enabled by default in Development, and it rejects consuming a scoped service from a singleton. Otherwise the singleton would capture one scoped instance for the app's lifetime (a captive dependency).

questions.prompt: An instance you create yourself and register with `AddSingleton(instance)` is disposed by the DI container when the app shuts down.
questions.explanation: False. The container disposes only the `IDisposable` services it created itself. Instances you construct and pass in are your responsibility to dispose.

questions.prompt: ASP.NET Core middleware runs in the order it is added in `Program.cs`, and the response passes back through it in reverse order.
questions.explanation: True. The pipeline is a chain of delegates: each middleware runs code, calls `next`, and then runs code on the way out. Order matters, for example authentication must come before authorization.

questions.prompt: A middleware that writes a response and does not call `next` short-circuits the pipeline, so the middleware registered after it never runs.
questions.explanation: True. Not calling the next delegate ends the request pipeline at that component. Static files middleware does this when it serves a file, for example.

questions.prompt: Middleware added with `app.Run` passes the request on to the middleware registered after it.
questions.explanation: False. `app.Run` adds terminal middleware: its delegate receives no `next` parameter, so anything registered after it is never reached for that branch.

questions.prompt: By default, entities returned by an EF Core query are tracked by the `DbContext`, so changes made to them are saved by `SaveChanges()`.
questions.explanation: True. Queries that return entity types are tracking queries by default. The change tracker detects modifications and writes them on `SaveChanges()`.

questions.prompt: Entities loaded with `AsNoTracking()` are written back to the database when you modify them and call `SaveChanges()`.
questions.explanation: False. No-tracking entities are not in the change tracker, so `SaveChanges()` ignores changes to them. You would have to attach them (e.g. `Update`) first; `AsNoTracking` is meant for read-only queries.

questions.prompt: Accessing a lazy-loaded navigation property inside a loop over N parent entities can send one extra database query per parent.
questions.explanation: True. This is the N+1 query problem: one query for the parents plus one per parent for the navigation. Eager loading with `Include` or a projection avoids it.

questions.prompt: EF Core lazy-loads navigation properties by default.
questions.explanation: False. Lazy loading is opt-in: you must use the proxies package with `UseLazyLoadingProxies()` or inject `ILazyLoader`. Without it, unloaded navigations simply stay null or empty.

questions.prompt: By default, EF Core loads an entity with several `Include`d collection navigations in a single SQL query, which can cause a cartesian explosion; `AsSplitQuery()` loads them with separate queries instead.
questions.explanation: True. Since EF Core 5, single-query mode is the default, and JOINing several collections duplicates rows. `AsSplitQuery()` (or a global setting) issues one query per collection at the cost of extra round trips.

questions.prompt: Looking up a key in a `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` is O(n) because it scans all entries.
questions.explanation: False. `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` is a hash table, so lookups by key are close to O(1) on average. Performance degrades only with a poor `GetHashCode` that causes many collisions.

questions.prompt: When adding an element to a `List<T>` exceeds its capacity, the list allocates a larger internal array and copies the existing elements into it.
questions.explanation: True. `List<T>` is backed by an array that grows (doubling) when full, which costs a copy. Setting an initial capacity avoids repeated reallocations when the size is known.

questions.prompt: `ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd(key, valueFactory)` guarantees the value factory runs at most once per key, even under concurrent calls.
questions.explanation: False. The factory runs outside the dictionary's locks, so concurrent callers may each invoke it, though only one result is stored and returned to all. Wrap values in `Lazy<T>` if the factory must run only once.

questions.prompt: Removing items from a `List<T>` inside a `foreach` loop over that same list is safe.
questions.explanation: False. The list's enumerator detects the modification and throws `InvalidOperationException` on the next iteration. Iterate backwards with a `for` loop or use `RemoveAll` instead.

questions.prompt: `Span<T>` is a `ref struct`, so it cannot be stored in a field of a class or used across an `await`.
questions.explanation: True. Ref structs must stay on the stack, so they cannot be boxed, be class fields, or live across `await` or `yield` boundaries. Use `Memory<T>` when you need to store or pass the buffer asynchronously.

questions.prompt: `"hello world".AsSpan(0, 5)` returns a `ReadOnlySpan<char>` over the original string's characters without allocating a new string.
questions.explanation: True. A span is a view over existing memory, so slicing only adjusts a reference and a length. `Substring`, by contrast, allocates a new string.

questions.prompt: An xUnit `[Theory]` with several `[InlineData]` attributes runs the test method once for each data row.
questions.explanation: True. `[Theory]` marks a parameterized test, and each `[InlineData]` supplies one set of arguments that is reported as a separate test case. `[Fact]` is for tests without parameters.

questions.prompt: xUnit creates a single instance of a test class and shares it across all its test methods, so fields set in one test are visible in the next.
questions.explanation: False. xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test, so the constructor acts as per-test setup. Shared state needs an explicit class fixture (`IClassFixture<T>`) or collection fixture.
